section.title: A Warning Against Adultery
section.sectionRationale: The fifth discourse gives the book's first sustained, single subject warning: the sweet but deadly words of the forbidden woman, verses 1 to 6, the ruin of the one who is seduced, verses 7 to 14, and, in deliberate contrast, the God given joy of faithful marriage, verses 15 to 20, closing with the LORD's all seeing eye over every path, verses 21 to 23.
section.thesis: The path to the forbidden woman looks sweet but ends in bitterness and ruin, while the path of faithful, joyful marriage is God's own good gift; both paths lie open before the eyes of the LORD, who examines every step.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the deceptive sweetness of the forbidden woman, verses 1 to 6; the devastating regret of the one who is seduced, verses 7 to 14; the call to rejoice instead in the wife of one's youth, verses 15 to 20; and the LORD's all seeing gaze over every path, verses 21 to 23.

units.label: The deceptive sweetness of the forbidden woman

verses.text: My son, pay attention to my wisdom; incline your ear to my insight,
that you may maintain discretion and your lips may preserve knowledge.
Though the lips of the {{zarah|forbidden woman}} drip honey and her speech is smoother than oil,
in the end she is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a double-edged sword.
Her feet go down to death; her steps lead straight to Sheol.
She does not consider the path of life; she does not know that her ways are unstable.

units.label: The regret of the one who is seduced

verses.text: So now, my sons, listen to me, and do not turn aside from the words of my mouth.
Keep your path far from her; do not go near the door of her house,
lest you concede your vigor to others, and your years to one who is cruel;
lest strangers feast on your wealth, and your labors enrich the house of a foreigner.
At the end of your life you will groan when your flesh and your body are spent,
and you will say, "How I hated {{musar|discipline}}, and my heart despised reproof!
I did not listen to the voice of my teachers or incline my ear to my mentors.
I am on the brink of utter ruin in the midst of the whole assembly."

units.label: Rejoice in the wife of your youth

verses.text: Drink water from your own cistern, and running water from your own well.
Why should your springs flow in the streets, your streams of water in the public squares?
Let them be yours alone, never to be shared with strangers.
May your fountain be blessed, and may you rejoice in the wife of your youth:
A loving doe, a graceful fawn, may her breasts satisfy you always; may you be {{shagah|captivated}} by her love forever.
Why be {{shagah|captivated}}, my son, by an adulteress, or embrace the bosom of a stranger?
For a man's ways are before the eyes of the LORD, and the LORD examines all his paths.
The iniquities of a wicked man entrap him; the cords of his sin entangle him.
He dies for lack of discipline, led astray by his own great folly.

zarah.gloss: The forbidden or strange woman, one who lures with smooth, honeyed speech that hides a bitter and deadly end. She appears repeatedly across chapters 2 through 7, always with the same pattern, sweet at first taste, ruinous in the end.

musar.gloss: Discipline or correction. The seduced man's greatest regret, voiced in verse 12, is not the pleasure he pursued but the discipline he despised and the teachers he refused to hear, showing that this ruin was preventable all along.

shagah.gloss: To be captivated, intoxicated, or led astray, the same root used for both proper and improper devotion in this passage. Verse 19 commands being captivated by one's own wife; verse 20 asks why a son would let himself be captivated, the identical word, by a woman not his own.

basic.context: This chapter is the book's first extended, single subject warning, and its subject is adultery. It paints the forbidden woman's words as honey that turns to bitter poison, pictures in devastating detail the regret of a man who ignored every warning, and then, in deliberate contrast, calls a husband to find deep and lasting joy in his own wife. The chapter ends by reminding the reader that the LORD sees every path, so no choice here is ever truly hidden.
basic.hermeneutics: This is direct moral instruction addressed to a young man, using vivid, sensory language, honey, oil, wormwood, a sword, to make an abstract danger feel immediate and real. Its warning is not against marriage or sexual desire, both are affirmed and even celebrated in verses 15 to 19, but against unfaithfulness, which the passage treats as a path that destroys the very things, vigor, wealth, reputation, and life itself, that it falsely promises to enrich.
basic.originalLanguages: The zarah, forbidden woman, is described with a taste metaphor, honey turning to wormwood, showing that her appeal is real but temporary and reversing. The son's deepest regret in verse 12 is hating musar, discipline, not merely the consequences of sin. And the same Hebrew root, shagah, describes being captivated both rightly, by one's own wife, verse 19, and wrongly, by an adulteress, verse 20, showing that the issue is not desire itself but its rightly or wrongly placed object.
basic.typology: The picture of a path that looks sweet but leads down to death and Sheol, verses 4 to 5, anticipates the New Testament's warning that sin, when it is full grown, brings forth death, James 1:15. The call to find joy exclusively in the wife of one's youth, verses 15 to 19, foreshadows the deeper union and exclusive devotion Paul later applies to Christ and the church, Ephesians 5:31 to 32.
basic.christ: This chapter's warning exposes a debt every human heart owes, since all have been captivated by wrong loves at some point, whether sexual or otherwise, and all deserve the entrapment described in verse 22. The gospel meets this exact problem: Christ was cut off, entangled in the cords of sin though He committed none, so that those bound by their own iniquities could be set free, and He calls His people, the bride He loves exclusively and eternally, to the same faithful, joyful devotion this chapter commends within marriage.
basic.god: God is the giver of marital joy, blessing the fountain and the wife of one's youth, verse 18, not merely tolerating desire but designing it for exclusive delight. He is also the all seeing judge, verse 21, before whom no secret path is ever truly hidden, and under whose moral order sin's own cords become the very trap that catches the sinner.
basic.crossReferences: James 1:15 traces the trajectory of sin to death, echoing verses 4 to 5. Hebrews 13:4 calls marriage to be held in honor and the marriage bed kept undefiled. Ephesians 5:31 to 32 applies exclusive marital union to Christ and the church. Galatians 6:7 to 8 states the same principle as verse 22, sowing to the flesh reaps corruption.
basic.oneStory: This chapter's warning against a sweet path that ends in death, and its celebration of joyful faithfulness instead, sits within Scripture's larger story of humanity's wandering hearts and God's persistent covenant love. That story reaches its center in Christ, who bore the entangling cords of sin for His unfaithful people and now calls them, His bride, to the same exclusive, joyful devotion this chapter commends between husband and wife.

context.literary:
Chapter 5 is built as a diptych with a hinge. Verses 1 to 14 are the warning, verses 15 to 20 are the invitation, and verses 21 to 23 give the reason that holds both together. The warning is itself in two parts. Verses 3 to 6 describe the woman, and verses 7 to 14 describe what her victim will say at the end. That second part is unusual, because the father gives his son a speech from the future, the groan of an old man looking back. The son hears his own regret before he has earned it.

The chapter is framed by the verb "to turn aside" and its relatives. At the start the son is told to pay attention and "incline your ear," verse 1, and at the close the man who would not listen is "led astray by his own great folly," verse 23. The same verb for being led astray, shagah, is used in verses 19 and 20 of the captivation of love, so the chapter moves from a good intoxication to a bad one and ends on the word that links them. Discipline frames it too. The man in the speech laments that he hated musar, verse 12, and the final line says he dies for lack of musar, verse 23.

Water carries the center. Verses 15 to 18 shift from the dry, bitter images of the forbidden woman to cisterns, wells, springs and fountains. The change of vocabulary is deliberate. Where she was honey that turned to wormwood and a sword, the wife is a fountain, a loving doe and a graceful fawn. The tone moves from the sharp to the generous without any change of speaker.

Finally, the chapter is the first of three sustained warnings on this theme in the opening collection, followed by Proverbs 6:20 to 35 and chapter 7. It sets up the book's pair of women, the forbidden woman and Lady Wisdom, who are given their final contrast in Proverbs 9.
context.historical:
Adultery in Israel was never a private matter. The law forbade it in the Ten Commandments, Exodus 20:14, and prescribed death for both parties, Leviticus 20:10 and Deuteronomy 22:22. That background lies behind the last line of the speech in verse 14, where the man is "on the brink of utter ruin in the midst of the whole assembly." The Hebrew words for the congregation are covenant terms, so the disgrace is the loss of standing in the community of the covenant people and not simply gossip.

Marriage was a covenant, and the prophets say so plainly. Malachi tells the men of his time that the LORD was a witness between them and "the wife of your youth," who was "your companion and your wife by covenant," Malachi 2:14. Proverbs 2:17 says of the forbidden woman that she "abandons the partner of her youth and forgets the covenant of her God." So the father's call to rejoice in the wife of one's youth means keeping a promise made before God.

The water language belongs to a dry land. Families dug cisterns in the rock to catch rain, and a well on one's own property was a prized asset. A spring flowing into the street was a waste, and a well shared with strangers could lead to quarrels. That helps the first hearers feel the image, as in Jeremiah's charge that Israel forsook the fountain of living water and dug broken cisterns, Jeremiah 2:13. Wealth, too, was counted in labor, and verse 10 pictures a lifetime's earnings going to the household of another.

If Solomon is the speaker, the chapter reads with a sad irony. His many foreign wives turned his heart from the LORD, 1 Kings 11:4, which is the kind of end this chapter warns against. The first readers were left to notice the warning and the failure side by side, and the book keeps both on the page.
context.canonical:
The chapter belongs to a cluster of warnings against the forbidden woman in the opening collection, Proverbs 2:16-19, 6:20-35 and 7:1-27, with Proverbs 9:13-18 giving Lady Folly her last word. The first of these already says that her house "sinks down to death" and that none who go to her return, Proverbs 2:18-19. Proverbs 7 gives the same road a name, "Her house is the road to Sheol," Proverbs 7:27, and shows a young man "lacking judgment" strolling toward her door at twilight, Proverbs 7:6-9.

The invitation to joy in marriage has its twin in the Song of Songs. There the bride's lips "drip sweetness like the honeycomb," Song of Songs 4:11, using the verb that Proverbs 5:3 gives to the adulteress. She is also "a garden locked up, a spring enclosed, a fountain sealed," Song of Songs 4:12, and "a well of fresh water," verse 15. The beloved can say, "I have come to my garden," Song of Songs 5:1. The images of Proverbs 5:15 to 19 are the same, and the Bible allows the richest language of desire to the faithful bed. Ecclesiastes agrees, "Enjoy life with your beloved wife," Ecclesiastes 9:9.

The New Testament carries the lines in two directions. Jesus takes the command against adultery to the eye and heart, Matthew 5:27-28, which is the logic of Proverbs 4:25 and 5:8. Paul tells the Corinthians to "flee from sexual immorality," 1 Corinthians 6:18, and tells the Thessalonians that each should control his own body "in holiness and honor," 1 Thessalonians 4:3-6. Hebrews says the marriage bed should be kept undefiled, Hebrews 13:4. James describes the path in the form of a staircase, desire, sin and death, James 1:14-15.

Verse 21 stands with the wider witness that God sees, Job 34:21, Proverbs 15:3 and Hebrews 4:13, and verse 22 with the image of the wicked caught in their own trap, Psalm 7:15-16 and Psalm 9:15.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The father is not trying to frighten his son out of desire. He is trying to give him a better thing to love than the thing that will ruin him. The chapter spends almost as many lines on joy in marriage as it does on the dangers of adultery, and the two halves are meant to be held together. A young man who only hears "no" will go looking for a "yes" elsewhere.

He wants the son to see a sequence and not just a moment. The honey comes first, then the bitterness, then the road to death. The woman in the first section is hardly described as a person. She is a pair of lips, a pair of feet and a house, because the father wants the son to look past the surface and see where she leads. That is why the warning shows the end of the story before the start. The old man's speech in verses 11 to 14 is a letter from the future, put into the young man's hands while he can still act.

The father also wants his son to understand what is at stake in ordinary terms. He names strength, years, wealth, the labor of a lifetime and a good name. Adultery looks like an affair of the moment, but it steals the whole shape of a life. Later in the book the cost is spelled out in a husband's fury, Proverbs 6:34, but here the harm is first of all to the man himself.

Finally, the father places everything before the eyes of the LORD. No part of the son's private life is outside the sphere of God's attention. The purpose of that last section is to keep the son from treating any secret choice as small.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is a mix of command and observation, and they need to be separated. The commands are plain: keep your path far from her, do not go near her door, drink from your own cistern, rejoice in the wife of your youth. The statements about outcomes, that strangers will feast on your wealth, that you will groan at the end, that his sins will entangle him, describe the grain of the moral world and not a fixed penalty applied by a court. Not every unfaithful person suffers in exactly these ways, and the proverb does not claim they do.

The celebration in verses 18 and 19 is not a command for every reader, because not every reader is married, but it is a permission and a blessing. It tells the unmarried that desire is not the enemy and the married that delight in one's spouse is godly. It is not a rule about duty or frequency. The words are the language of love poetry, and they should be read warmly.

One caution belongs here. The picture of a seductive woman should not be used to excuse men or to blame women for men's choices. The father's instruction puts the responsibility on the son, who is told to keep his path far from her and not to go near her door, verse 8. The New Testament states the standard for both sexes, 1 Corinthians 7:2-5, and Jesus lays the guilt on the one who looks with lust, Matthew 5:28. The proverb also leaves room for the person who has already fallen. The gospel tells of washing and forgiveness for those who were once sexually immoral or adulterers, 1 Corinthians 6:9-11, and of Jesus saying to a woman taken in adultery, "Then neither do I condemn you... Now go and sin no more," John 8:11.

debates.question: Is this chapter's warning relevant only to men, since it addresses 'my son'?

views.label: Addressed specifically to young men in a patriarchal setting
views.case: The passage's direct address and its picture of the tempting woman reflect the book's consistent father to son form of address throughout chapters 1 to 9.

views.label: A principle that applies to both sexes
views.case: The underlying moral claims, that sexual sin promises sweetness and delivers ruin, that faithful marriage is God's good gift, and that the LORD sees every path, apply without remainder to women as much as men, even though the literary form addresses a son.

debates.bearing: The specific literary address to a son reflects its ancient setting, but its moral substance, guard against sexual temptation and treasure faithful marriage, binds all people, and the New Testament applies the same standard of faithfulness to both husbands and wives alike, 1 Corinthians 7:2-5.

debates.question: Is verse 16 a question about waste or a promise of overflow?

views.label: A rhetorical question, as the BSB has it
views.case: The verse follows 'drink water from your own cistern,' so the question asks why a man's springs should flow into the streets. The point is that his love should not be spread among strangers, and verse 17 backs this up by saying they should be his alone, never shared.

views.label: A statement of blessing and fruitfulness
views.case: Older English translations read it as a statement, that the springs will overflow into the streets. On this reading the image points to the blessing of children and a household whose life spills out to others, and the chapter turns to exclusivity only in verse 17. The Hebrew can be read both ways.

debates.bearing: The BSB's reading fits the immediate flow best, because the surrounding verses press for exclusive faithfulness. Yet the second reading catches something the whole chapter affirms, that faithful love is meant to be fruitful and generous. Either way, the proverb treats love as a spring that is kept for the one for whom it is meant.

debates.question: Who is the 'forbidden woman' of verse 3?

views.label: A real adulteress or foreign woman
views.case: The Hebrew word zarah means a stranger or outsider, and the BSB footnote offers 'adulteress' in verse 3 and 'a foreign woman or another man's wife' in verse 20. The setting is a young man's daily life, and the damage described, loss of wealth, shame in the assembly and early death, fits actual adultery.

views.label: A personification of Folly
views.case: The book sets this woman beside Lady Wisdom, and Proverbs 9:13-18 gives Folly a house, a loud voice and an invitation. On this reading the figure represents every seductive alternative to wisdom, so that the chapter speaks of any false love as well as sexual sin.

views.label: Both a literal danger and a figure of folly
views.case: Many see the figure as working on both levels, a real temptation drawn with the colors of the book's larger contrast between wisdom and folly.

debates.bearing: The chapter's practical details, a door, a house, a husband's household and a wife of one's youth, make the literal reading unavoidable. The book's larger design makes the figurative reading likely as well. Taking both seriously keeps the warning concrete while still letting the passage speak about every counterfeit of wisdom.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter turns on a small group of verbs and nouns whose connections do not survive translation. The first is the verb in verse 3, which the BSB renders "drip." It is the same verb used in Song of Songs 4:11 for the bride's lips, which "drip sweetness like the honeycomb." The warning and the celebration share their vocabulary. What is a sweet gift from one woman is a poisonous bait from the other, and the difference lies in the covenant, not in the words. The next verse gives the counterpart, wormwood, la'anah, a bitter plant that Scripture uses as a figure for the fruit of turning away from the LORD, as in Deuteronomy 29:18, where a "root" bears "poisonous and bitter fruit."

In verse 6 the BSB says she does "not consider the path of life." The verb behind it, palas, means to level, weigh or ponder. It is the verb in Proverbs 4:26, where the son is told to "make a level path," and the BSB footnote on 4:26 offers "Ponder the path for your feet." It returns at 5:21, where the LORD "examines" all his paths, and the footnote there reads "ponders or makes level." The woman does not weigh her road, the son is told to weigh his, and the LORD weighs everyone's. The chapter makes God the final examiner of the thing the woman neglects.

The word translated "forbidden woman" is zarah, which means a stranger or outsider, and the same root gives the plural "strangers" in verses 10 and 17. The words work like a chain. Strangers feast on your wealth, your springs must not be shared with strangers, and the zarah is the stranger who brings it about. The BSB footnotes show the range, "the adulteress" at 5:3 and "a foreign woman or another man's wife" at 5:20.

The word for "captivated" in verses 19 and 20 is shagah, a verb that means to stray, reel or be intoxicated. It is a word for wandering. In Proverbs it is used of the drunkard who is "led astray" by wine, and here of love. The BSB footnote at verse 19 records "be led astray." The most important thing about the word is that it appears again in verse 23, where the man is "led astray by his own great folly." The final verse ends on the same verb that opened the praise of marriage, so the whole chapter asks one question: by what will you allow yourself to be carried away?

Finally, the BSB's "love" in verse 19 is given as a doe and a fawn, ayelet and ya'alat chen. The second phrase contains chen, grace or charm, the word the book uses for the garland of grace in Proverbs 1:9 and 4:9. The wife is described in the vocabulary of wisdom's own gifts. The point is not subtle. Faithful love is among the graces that wisdom offers.

typology.type: The sweet path that leads down to death and Sheol, Proverbs 5:4-5
typology.fulfillment: The father says the woman's feet go down to death and her steps lead straight to Sheol, and Proverbs 7:27 says her house is 'the road to Sheol.' James traces the same movement from desire to sin to death, James 1:14-15, and Paul says 'the wages of sin is death,' Romans 6:23. In Christ the road is reversed. He went down into death and came out of it, 'You will not abandon my soul to Sheol,' Psalm 16:10, and He says, 'I hold the keys of Death and of Hades,' Revelation 1:18. The type shows where sin leads, and it falls short only in that it cannot say who can bring a person back. The gospel does.

typology.type: The cisterns and the fountain, Proverbs 5:15-18
typology.fulfillment: The father sets faithful love beside a spring that belongs to one household. Jeremiah applies the picture to Israel, who forsook 'the fountain of living water' and dug 'broken cisterns that cannot hold water,' Jeremiah 2:13. In the Gospel of John, Jesus offers living water to the woman at the well, John 4:10-14, and cries out in the temple that anyone who is thirsty should come to Him and drink, John 7:37-38. The pictures are not the same, since Proverbs is about marriage and Jeremiah and John are about God, but they share one idea. Thirst is met by the true source and not by borrowed waters. The proverb's cistern is a lesser sign of what Christ gives without limit.

typology.type: The wife of one's youth and a covenant kept, Proverbs 5:18
typology.fulfillment: God calls Israel His wife and calls her back 'like the rejected wife of one's youth,' Isaiah 54:6, and promises, 'I will betroth you to Me forever,' Hosea 2:19-20. Paul quotes Genesis 2:24 and says of the one flesh union that he is speaking of Christ and the church, Ephesians 5:31-32. Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her, Ephesians 5:25-27, and the Bible ends with the marriage of the Lamb, Revelation 19:7. Human marriage is a real covenant and a sign of that union. The type falls short because the Bridegroom of the gospel does not leave or fail, and He keeps faith even with a bride who has not.

typology.type: The one entangled in the cords of his own sin, Proverbs 5:22
typology.fulfillment: The wicked man is held fast by cords he made himself, a figure also found in Psalm 9:15, where the feet of the nations are caught in the net they hid. Paul writes that Christ 'redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13, and that the record of debt standing against us was nailed to the cross, Colossians 2:14. The proverb describes a trap that cannot be undone by the one caught in it. The gospel supplies the release, in that another takes on the debt and breaks the cords. The link rests on the theme of bondage and release, not on a statement in the proverb itself, so it should be held as an echo and not as a prediction.

study.christ:
This chapter shows a human problem that the gospel exists to answer, and it also gives the Bible one of its most important pictures of the Savior as a husband. Start with the problem. The father says the wicked man's own iniquities entrap him and the cords of his sin hold him fast, verse 22. That is a description of a person who cannot get free by trying. Jesus says as much when He tells His hearers that whoever practices sin is a slave to sin, John 8:34. The proverb gives no rescue, only a warning, and it leaves the reader looking for the One who can cut cords.

He has come. The New Testament says Christ redeemed us from the curse by becoming a curse for us, Galatians 3:13, and that the record of debt standing against us has been nailed to the cross, Colossians 2:14. Where Proverbs ends on a man who "dies for lack of discipline," verse 23, the gospel tells of One who bore the full cost of the world's unfaithfulness and came back from it. Death and Sheol, the destination of the forbidden woman's road in verse 5, are exactly what the risen Christ claims to hold, "I hold the keys of Death and of Hades," Revelation 1:18. The path that goes down has a Master who has been down and returned.

Next, the picture of marriage. The father's praise of the wife of one's youth is a real picture of faithful human love, and the Bible uses it for something greater. God calls His people His wife, Isaiah 54:5-6, and promises, "I will betroth you to Me forever," Hosea 2:19-20. Paul says that Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her, to make her holy and present her without stain, Ephesians 5:25-27, and that the one flesh union of Genesis 2:24 speaks of Christ and the church, Ephesians 5:31-32. John the Baptist calls Jesus the bridegroom, John 3:29, and Paul tells the Corinthians he has betrothed them to one husband, 2 Corinthians 11:2. The husband of Proverbs 5 is told to be captivated by his wife's love always. Christ is the Husband who is, in the fullest sense, faithful to a wife who has often wandered.

Then there is the question of the person who has already walked the road. The chapter holds out little for the man who has ended in ruin, and the gospel supplies what Proverbs only hints at. Paul lists adulterers among those who will not inherit the kingdom, and then adds, "And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ," 1 Corinthians 6:9-11. Jesus tells the woman caught in adultery that He does not condemn her and sends her out to sin no more, John 8:11. He does not lower the standard of Matthew 5:28. He carries its weight Himself and then gives a new beginning.

A word of care. The woman in Proverbs 5 is not a code for something else, and the chapter is not a prediction about Jesus. The links are made by the New Testament's own use of marriage, bondage and death. They show that the longing for faithful love and for release from cords is answered in Christ, and they invite readers to see the chapter's warnings as signposts toward Him.
study.god:
The chapter's final verses state the doctrine outright. "A man's ways are before the eyes of the LORD, and the LORD examines all his paths," verse 21. God sees what the young man would hide. The same truth is stated in the Psalms, "You are aware of all my ways," Psalm 139:3, and in Job, "His eyes are on the ways of a man, and He sees his every step," Job 34:21. The word "examines" is a verb of weighing, the same verb used for the road the woman fails to ponder. God does what the adulteress will not do. He thinks carefully about every path.

That is a comfort and a warning at once. For the person who is tempted, it means no secret is truly private, and the knowledge of a watching God is the oldest safeguard against sin. Joseph's answer to his master's wife, "How could I do such a great evil and sin against God?" Genesis 39:9, shows what this knowledge does for a person. For the person who has been wronged, the same truth means no betrayal goes unseen. The God who sees is the One who will judge, and the New Testament says so plainly, "the Lord will avenge all such acts," 1 Thessalonians 4:6.

The chapter shows God as the author of marital joy and not only as its guardian. The praise of the wife in verses 18 and 19 makes no apology, and Scripture elsewhere says that God "richly provides all things for us to enjoy," 1 Timothy 6:17. Delight in a spouse is received as a gift from His hand. The first marriage was His doing, Genesis 2:22-24, and the blessing to be fruitful came from Him. A holy God is not the enemy of desire. He is the One who designed it for covenant love and who guards it by drawing a line.

The chapter also shows that God builds consequence into the world. The sinner's own iniquities trap him, and his own folly leads him astray, verses 22 and 23. This is not a God who stands apart and then acts occasionally against the guilty. The moral order He made carries its own verdicts, as Paul says, "A man reaps what he sows," Galatians 6:7. Behind that order stands a personal God who sees and who judges.

Finally, God is a covenant witness. Malachi says the LORD was "a witness between you and the wife of your youth," Malachi 2:14, and Proverbs 2:17 says the forbidden woman forgets "the covenant of her God." Marriage is therefore a promise made in His presence. In worship the chapter asks us to thank Him for marriage and for faithful friends, to confess the ways we have been led astray by lesser loves, and to bring our hidden paths into the light, since they were never hidden from Him.

crossReferences.note: The bride's lips 'drip sweetness like the honeycomb,' using the verb that Proverbs 5:3 gives to the adulteress, and she is 'a garden locked up, a spring enclosed, a fountain sealed.' The Song confirms that the father's images of honey and fountain are rightly used for faithful love, and shows what the forbidden woman only imitates.

The LORD is called a witness between a man and 'the wife of your youth,' who is his companion and wife by covenant. The prophet's wording is close to the phrase in verse 18 and shows that the father's counsel is a call to keep a covenant made before God and not only to stay out of trouble.

The first warning against the forbidden woman says she abandons the partner of her youth and forgets the covenant of her God, and that her house sinks down to death. It gives the covenant background for chapter 5 and shows that the book has been building this warning from its first lectures.

A young man 'lacking judgment' walks near her corner at twilight, strolling toward her house. The scene shows verse 8 in action, since he has not kept his path far from her door. The two chapters together show how temptation is approached by degrees and not by a single leap.

Declares, 'Her house is the road to Sheol, descending to the chambers of death.' It repeats the claim of 5:5 almost as a chorus, that her steps lead down to Sheol. The book keeps returning to the destination, because the young man is more likely to see where a road ends than where it begins.

Says marriage should be honored by all and the marriage bed kept undefiled, and that God will judge the sexually immoral and the adulterer. It joins the chapter's two halves in a single sentence, celebrating marriage and warning against adultery, and it ties the warning to God's judgment as verse 21 does.

Paul tells the Corinthians to flee sexual immorality and says the person who sins sexually sins against his own body. The command to flee matches the father's command to keep far from her door. Paul adds a new reason, that the believer's body belongs to Christ, 1 Corinthians 6:19-20.

Jesus takes the command against adultery to the eye and the heart. He agrees with the father's emphasis that the road begins long before the door. Verse 8 tells the son to stay far, and Jesus teaches that the first step is a look that desires.

Describes temptation as being lured and enticed, desire conceiving and giving birth to sin, and sin when full grown giving birth to death. It reads like a commentary on verses 3 to 5, with the honey, the road and Sheol. The New Testament sees the same life cycle in every kind of sin.

Joseph refuses his master's wife by asking how he could do such a great evil and sin against God. He is the proverb in practice. His reason is the one given in verse 21, that his ways are before the LORD, and his action is the one given in verse 8, which is to flee and keep away.

God charges Israel with forsaking the fountain of living water and digging broken cisterns. The prophet takes the language of water and thirst that Proverbs 5 applies to marriage and turns it toward the people's unfaithfulness to God. It shows that the chapter's fountain imagery has a larger background in the covenant.

Paul quotes the creation text on the one flesh union and says it speaks of Christ and the church. The father's counsel to be satisfied with the wife of one's youth is lifted into a picture of Christ's exclusive love for His people, and the faithfulness the chapter asks of husbands is grounded in His.

study.oneStory:
Proverbs 5 stands in a story that begins with a wedding. In Genesis 2 God brings the woman to the man and the narrator says that "they will become one flesh," Genesis 2:24, and that they were naked and not ashamed. The first marriage is the pattern for this chapter's praise of the wife of one's youth. When Genesis 3 follows with the fall, desire and shame come into the picture together, and every later warning about unfaithfulness is a reply to that fracture. Proverbs 5 tells the young man how to live east of Eden without letting the loss define him, by protecting the one covenant that still carries something of the garden.

The chapter also moves with Israel's story. The prophets use marriage as the central image of the covenant. The LORD is the husband, Israel the wife, and Israel's idolatry is adultery, as in Hosea and Jeremiah. The honey and bitterness of verses 3 and 4 come to describe the nation's long flirtation with other gods, and the cisterns of verse 15 recall Jeremiah's broken cisterns. The father's warnings to a son become, in the prophets, God's grief over a faithless people, and also His promise, "I will betroth you to Me forever," Hosea 2:19-20.

The story reaches its center in Christ. He is the faithful Husband who gave Himself for His bride, Ephesians 5:25-27, who holds the keys to Death and Hades, Revelation 1:18, and who frees those caught in the cords of sin, Galatians 3:13. He speaks forgiveness over people who have walked the wrong road, John 8:11, and then calls them to a life of faithful love in a new body, 1 Corinthians 6:9-11.

The story ends with a wedding too. The marriage of the Lamb has come and His bride has made herself ready, Revelation 19:7, and she is a city adorned for her husband, Revelation 21:2. In the new creation the thirsty are given water from the spring of the water of life, Revelation 21:6, and the longing that Proverbs 5 describes in the language of fountains is fully satisfied. The father's hope for his son, to be captivated by love that is faithful and good, is realized in a people who are held forever by the love of Christ, and the wayward wandering of Genesis finally comes to rest in a home.

sermon.title: Warning against Adultery
sermon.why: Begg walks directly through Proverbs 5, the exact passage of this study, warning of the consequences of infidelity and pointing to the joy of marital faithfulness as God's ordained gift, matching the chapter's own structure and aim.

quiz.q: How does the chapter describe the forbidden woman's appeal and its true end, verses 3 to 5?

options.text: Her words are sweet as honey at first, but in the end she is bitter as wormwood and leads to death.
options.note: This is the exact contrast the passage draws.

options.text: She offers no real appeal at all, only obvious danger.
options.note: The passage stresses her real, deceptive sweetness, not obvious repulsiveness.

options.text: She is dangerous only because of social gossip.
options.note: The danger described is far deeper, spiritual and mortal, not merely reputational.

options.text: Her appeal fades quickly but carries no lasting consequence.
options.note: The passage's point is the opposite, the appeal reverses into bitterness with lasting, even fatal, consequence.

quiz.q: What does the seduced man regret most, according to verses 12 to 13?

options.text: That he hated discipline and refused to listen to his teachers.
options.note: This is stated directly as his central regret, not merely the outward consequences.

options.text: That he was never warned at all.
options.note: The passage shows he was taught and warned but refused to listen.

options.text: That his family was too strict with him.
options.note: The passage places responsibility on his own refusal to listen, not on excessive parental strictness.

options.text: That he lacked the resources to succeed in life.
options.note: Financial loss is mentioned, verse 10, but his own stated regret centers on despising discipline, not resources.

quiz.q: What positive picture does the chapter give in verses 15 to 19?

options.text: Joyful, exclusive delight in the wife of one's youth, pictured as drinking from one's own well.
options.note: This is the chapter's positive alternative to the forbidden woman.

options.text: A command to avoid marriage altogether.
options.note: The passage celebrates marriage; it does not discourage it.

options.text: Permission to share intimacy widely as long as it is not called adultery.
options.note: The passage explicitly commands exclusivity, let them be yours alone, the opposite of sharing widely.

options.text: A picture of duty without any real joy.
options.note: The passage's language, rejoice, captivated, satisfy, is emotionally rich, not merely dutiful.

quiz.q: What does verse 21 say about the LORD's awareness of human conduct?

options.text: A man's ways are before the eyes of the LORD, who examines all his paths.
options.note: This is the exact statement, grounding the whole warning in God's all seeing justice.

options.text: God is unaware of private choices made in secret.
options.note: The verse states the opposite, nothing is hidden from Him.

options.text: God only judges public actions, not private ones.
options.note: The verse specifically emphasizes that all paths, including private ones, are examined by God.

options.text: God's awareness applies only to Israel's leaders.
options.note: The statement is general, about any man's ways, not limited to leaders.

quiz.q: How does this chapter's warning connect to the gospel?

options.text: It exposes a universal danger of misplaced devotion that Christ answers by bearing sin's entangling judgment and calling His people to faithful love.
options.note: This connects the chapter's warning and positive vision to Christ's atoning work and His relationship to the church, Ephesians 5:31-32.

options.text: It has no meaningful connection to the gospel.
options.note: The chapter's themes of sin, judgment, and faithful covenant love connect directly to the gospel's own categories.

options.text: It teaches that only sexual sins matter to God.
options.note: This chapter's specific focus is sexual faithfulness, but Scripture treats it as one of many entangling sins, not the sole concern of God.

options.text: It shows marriage is unnecessary once someone is in Christ.
options.note: The New Testament instead honors marriage highly, even using it as a picture of Christ and the church, rather than treating it as unnecessary.

questions: The forbidden woman's words are sweet at first and bitter in the end. Where in your own life have you seen a tempting shortcut promise pleasure and deliver regret instead?
The seduced man's deepest regret was hating discipline and ignoring his teachers. Is there current correction or counsel you are resisting that you may deeply regret ignoring later?

Verses 15 to 19 celebrate joyful, exclusive delight in marriage as God's good gift. If you are married, how are you actively cultivating that joy rather than taking it for granted or looking elsewhere?
Verse 21 says the LORD examines every path, even the hidden ones. How does knowing that God sees everything change what you do when no one else is watching?

Christ bore the entangling judgment of sin so unfaithful people could be set free and calls His church to faithful, joyful devotion. Where do you need His grace today for a wandering heart, whether in marriage or in some other area of misplaced desire?

translationNotes.note: Forbidden woman can also be rendered the adulteress; smoother than oil, or her palate, pictures speech so pleasant it seems to promise nothing but good.

May you be captivated renders a Hebrew verb that can also mean be led astray; the same root appears in verse 20 for wrongful captivation, forming a deliberate wordplay between rightly and wrongly placed devotion.
Stranger here, as in verse 10, can also be rendered a foreign woman or another man's wife, reinforcing that the danger is a woman outside the bond of one's own marriage covenant.
